rv.q: Which means that it needs the sort of four-star turns it gets from Evans, a magnificent Sheila Hancock as his ruthless mum and a committed Keeley Hawes as his WAG-ish wife.
Exton’s stop-go plotting and the sagging patches in Harry Burton’s production prevent the material from developing any comic momentum.
But to me it felt a terrible waste of a strong cast.
I incline to the view that this is because it isn’t much good.

No such defence can be mounted for this new play by the late Clive Exton , whose work for ITV's Armchair Theatre in the 1960s pioneered a new form of black comedy, and who went on to write for Jeeves and Wooster and Poirot .
But what should be played as fast-moving farce feels much longer than its two-and-a-quarter hours, and even the swearing becomes tiresome after a while.
It's just irredeemably and gloriously bad.

cn.t: Critics largely pan this foul-mouthed Essex farce as brash and unfunny, despite a game cast. Lee Evans earns rare praise, but most find Exton's posthumous comedy too crude to land its jokes.
